title: Windows 11 WSL Hacking Setup: Build a Complete Penetration Testing Lab
excerpt: Turn your Windows 11 machine into a powerful penetration testing workstation using WSL2, Kali Linux, and essential security tools — no dual-boot required.
content:
If you are a penetration tester, security researcher, or someone learning cybersecurity on a Windows machine, you do not need to dual-boot or carry a separate laptop. Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 (WSL2) gives you a full Linux kernel running inside Windows with near-native performance. Combined with the right tools and configuration, your Windows 11 machine becomes a legitimate hacking workstation.

This guide walks you through the entire setup — from enabling WSL to configuring networking, installing Kali Linux, setting up essential tools, and hardening your lab environment.

Chapter 1: Why WSL2 for Hacking

WSL2 is not a virtual machine in the traditional sense. It runs a real Linux kernel inside a lightweight Hyper-V virtual machine, but integrates so deeply with Windows that it feels native. You can access Windows files from Linux at /mnt/c/ and access Linux files from Windows through the network path \\wsl$\.

Advantages over dual-boot: Run Windows and Linux simultaneously. Copy-paste between environments. Share files instantly. No reboot required. Use Windows tools (Burp Suite, Nmap Windows) alongside Linux tools. Access Windows WiFi adapters for wireless testing through USB passthrough.

Advantages over traditional VMs: Near-native file system performance (NTFS operations are fast). Lower memory overhead. Better GPU integration. Automatic startup with Windows. No need to manage virtual disks manually.

Chapter 2: Enabling WSL2 on Windows 11

Open PowerShell as Administrator and run: wsl --install

This command enables the required Windows features (Virtual Machine Platform and Windows Subsystem for Linux), downloads the latest Linux kernel, sets WSL2 as the default version, and installs Ubuntu by default.

If you want more control, enable features manually:

dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux /all /norestart

dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:VirtualMachinePlatform /all /norestart

After enabling, restart your computer. Then set WSL2 as default: wsl --set-default-version 2

Verify your installation: wsl --list --verbose

You should see your installed distributions with VERSION 2. If any show VERSION 1, convert them: wsl --set-version DistroName 2

Chapter 3: Installing Kali Linux

Kali Linux is the industry standard for penetration testing. Microsoft provides an official WSL image that integrates with the Windows Store.

Install from PowerShell: wsl --install -d kali-linux

Or install from the Microsoft Store — search for Kali Linux and click Install.

On first launch, you will be prompted to create a root user. Set a strong password immediately.

Update your system: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y

Install the Kali metapackage for a full tool set: sudo apt install -y kali-linux-large

For a lighter setup, install individual tools as needed rather than the full metapackage. The kali-linux-large metapackage is about 5GB and includes most commonly used tools.

Chapter 4: Alternative Distributions

Parrot OS: Lighter than Kali, includes privacy tools alongside security tools. Install from the Microsoft Store or download the WSL tarball from parrotsec.org and import with: wsl --import Parrot C:\WSL\Parrot parrot-rootfs.tar.gz

Ubuntu + Manual Tools: If you want a clean slate, install Ubuntu and build your own toolkit. This gives you full control over what is installed. Use: wsl --install -d ubuntu

BlackArch: Arch-based with 2800+ security tools. Install on top of Arch WSL: wsl --install -d archlinux, then follow the BlackArch bootstrap installer.

For most users, Kali from the Microsoft Store is the easiest path. It auto-updates and integrates cleanly.

Chapter 5: Essential Configuration

Update Kali packages regularly: sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade

Install common utilities: sudo apt install -y curl wget git vim tmux zsh net-tools dnsutils whois nmap

Shell setup: Install Oh My Zsh for a better terminal experience: sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)"

Fix Chinese/Japanese font rendering: If you see boxes instead of characters in some tools, install: sudo apt install fonts-noto-cjk

Fix tab completion: Add to your .zshrc or .bashrc: complete -C /usr/bin/nmap nmap and source ~/.zshrc

Chapter 6: Networking in WSL2

This is where WSL2 gets tricky for security work. WSL2 runs in a NAT network by default, meaning your Linux instance has a different IP address than your Windows host. This matters for port forwarding, reverse shells, and VPN connections.

Find your WSL IP: hostname -I or ip addr show eth0

Find your Windows IP from WSL: cat /etc/resolv.conf | grep nameserver

Port forwarding from Windows to WSL: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=8080 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=8080 connectaddress=$(wsl hostname -I | awk '{print $1}')

View existing port forwards: netsh interface portproxy show all

Remove a port forward: netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenport=8080 listenaddress=0.0.0.0

Firewall rule to allow forwarded ports: New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "WSL Port 8080" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 8080 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow

VPN considerations: WSL2 does not automatically use VPN connections from Windows. To route WSL traffic through a VPN, you need to manually set the default gateway. Find the VPN interface gateway and run: sudo ip route add default via GATEWAY_IP

For persistent VPN routing, create a script that runs on VPN connect. Alternatively, use a split tunnel VPN that routes only specific subnets through the tunnel.

Chapter 7: USB Device Passthrough

If you need to use USB WiFi adapters for wireless attacks or USB rubber ducky devices, WSL2 supports USB passthrough through usbipd-win.

Install usbipd on Windows: winget install usbipd

List USB devices: usbipd list

Bind a device: usbipd bind --busid 1-3 (replace with your device bus ID)

Attach to WSL: usbipd attach --wsl --busid 1-3

Inside WSL, verify: lsusb

This works for WiFi adapters (Alfa AWUS036ACH, etc.), but note that some adapters have driver issues in WSL. Check compatibility before buying. For wireless testing, a dedicated Linux machine or a VM with USB passthrough may be more reliable.

Chapter 8: GPU Passthrough for Hashcat

WSL2 supports GPU computing through CUDA, which means you can run Hashcat with GPU acceleration for password cracking.

On Windows: Install the latest NVIDIA GPU driver from nvidia.com (not from Device Manager). WSL2 uses a special driver that bridges the Windows and Linux drivers.

Inside WSL: sudo apt install -y nvidia-cuda-toolkit

Verify GPU access: nvidia-smi

Install Hashcat: sudo apt install -y hashcat

Test GPU cracking: hashcat -b (benchmark)

This gives you full GPU-accelerated hash cracking without leaving Windows. The performance is nearly identical to native Linux because WSL2 shares the GPU driver with Windows.

Chapter 9: Setting Up a Hacking Lab Network

For practice, you need vulnerable targets. Here is how to set up a local lab network inside WSL2.

Install Docker in WSL: sudo apt install -y docker.io && sudo usermod -aG docker $USER && newgrp docker

Create a lab network: docker network create --subnet=172.20.0.0/16 labnet

Run vulnerable containers:

docker run -d --name metasploitable --net labnet --ip 172.20.0.10 metasploitable2

docker run -d --name dvwa --net labnet --ip 172.20.0.11 -p 80:80 vulnerables/web-dvwa

docker run -d --name juice-shop --net labnet --ip 172.20.0.12 -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop

Access from Windows: Since the containers are in the WSL2 network, you can access them through port forwarding or directly if you set up the WSL network as bridged.

Download vulnerable VMs: Import VulnerHack, OWASP WebGoat, or TryHackMeAttackBox as OVA files into VirtualBox on Windows. These run alongside WSL for a complete lab environment.

Chapter 10: Tool Configuration

Nmap: Works out of the box in WSL2. For OS detection, you may need to run with sudo. SYN scans work without additional configuration.

Burp Suite: Run the Windows version alongside WSL. Configure your browser to proxy through 127.0.0.1:8080. For tools running in WSL that need to reach Burp, set HTTP_PROXY=http://$(cat /etc/resolv.conf | grep nameserver | awk '{print $2}'):8080

Metasploit: sudo msfdb init to set up the database. sudo msfconsole to start. Works fully in WSL2 with no special configuration.

John the Ripper: sudo apt install -y john. For GPU support, build from source with CUDA support: git clone https://github.com/openwall/john && cd john/src && ./configure && make

SQLMap: sudo apt install -y sqlmap. Works natively. For best results, use with Tor: sudo apt install -y tor && sudo systemctl start tor && sqlmap -u "TARGET" --tor --tor-type=SOCKS5

Wireshark: Install the Windows version. WSL2 does not support packet capture natively. Use Windows Wireshark to capture traffic on your interfaces, or use tcpdump inside WSL for basic analysis: sudo apt install -y tcpdump && sudo tcpdump -i eth0

Hashcat: See the GPU passthrough chapter. Install with sudo apt install -y hashcat and run hashcat -b to verify GPU acceleration.

Chapter 11: Performance Tuning

WSL2 is configured with conservative defaults. Tune these for a better hacking experience.

Increase memory allocation: Create %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig with:

[wsl2]
memory=8GB
processors=4
swap=4GB
localhostForwarding=true

Move your workspace to ext4: File operations on /mnt/c are slow because they cross the Windows/Linux boundary. Keep your working files on the Linux filesystem at /home/youruser/ for 10x faster performance.

Disable Windows Defender scanning of WSL: Add exclusions for the WSL virtual disk path. Open Windows Security, go to Virus and Threat Protection, Manage Settings, Exclusions, and add: C:\Users\YourUser\AppData\Local\Packages\ (find the Kali folder inside).

Use tmux: Install tmux and run long processes in sessions. This prevents disconnection when your terminal closes. tmux new -s recon starts a new session named recon. tmux attach -t recon reattaches.

Chapter 12: Daily Workflow

A professional workflow keeps your tools organized and your findings documented.

Project structure:

mkdir -p ~/projects/{target_name}/{recon,exploits,loot,notes}

Documentation: Keep a running notes file for each engagement. Use Markdown: vim ~/projects/target/notes/findings.md

Tool organization: Create aliases in your shell config for frequently used commands: alias nmap-full='nmap -sC -sV -oN full_scan.txt -p- TARGET'

Parallel scanning: Run multiple tools simultaneously using tmux panes. Split your terminal: Ctrl+B then % for vertical split, Ctrl+B then " for horizontal split.

Results management: Always save tool output to files with timestamps: date +%Y%m%d_nmap_output.txt. This creates an audit trail for your findings.

Chapter 13: Common Issues and Fixes

WSL crashing or hanging: Run wsl --shutdown from PowerShell to force restart. If persistent, increase memory in .wslconfig and disable memory compression: Disable-MMAgent -MemoryCompression

DNS resolution failing: Echo nameserver 8.8.8.8 | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf. For a permanent fix, add to .wslconfig: [network] generateResolvConf=false, then set your DNS manually.

Port forwarding not working: Check Windows Firewall rules. Verify netsh portproxy rules are correct. Test with curl from inside WSL: curl localhost:PORT

Slow file operations: Move files to the Linux filesystem (/home/user/) instead of working on /mnt/c/. The WSL2 VM uses ext4 natively and NTFS operations are slow through the 9P protocol.

NVIDIA GPU not detected: Reinstall the Windows GPU driver. Do not install the Linux NVIDIA driver from apt — it conflicts with the WSL CUDA bridge. Use nvidia-cuda-toolkit from apt instead.

Chapter 14: Security Hardening

Your hacking lab is also a system that needs to be secured.

Snapshot before破坏: Before running dangerous exploits, export your WSL distribution: wsl --export kali kali-backup.tar. Import it later if things break: wsl --import kali-restored C:\WSL\kali-restored kali-backup.tar

Network isolation: Do not expose WSL services to the internet. Use localhost forwarding only. Disable WSL automatic port forwarding if not needed.

File permissions: Even in WSL, use proper Linux permissions. Never run tools as root unless necessary. Use sudo for specific commands, not entire sessions.

Keep updated: Regularly update both Windows and your WSL distributions. Security patches fix vulnerabilities in the WSL kernel and integration layer.

Separate accounts: Use a dedicated Windows account for security work. Do not mix personal browsing with penetration testing activities.

Conclusion

WSL2 has transformed how security professionals work on Windows. You get the full power of Linux tools, the convenience of Windows applications, and the performance of near-native execution. The setup takes about an hour, and the result is a versatile workstation that handles reconnaissance, exploitation, post-exploitation, and reporting without rebooting or switching machines.

The key to getting the most out of this setup is practice. Build your lab, break things, fix them, and document your workflow. The better your environment, the more effective your testing will be. Start with the basics, add tools as you need them, and always keep your systems updated. Your Windows 11 machine with WSL2 is not a compromise — it is a legitimate security workstation.

title: The Complete Guide to Learning Linux from Zero to Advanced
excerpt: A comprehensive roadmap covering everything from your first terminal command to system administration, networking, security, and shell scripting.
content:
Linux runs the majority of the internet, powers every Android phone, runs on supercomputers, and is the backbone of cloud computing. Whether you want to become a sysadmin, a security professional, a DevOps engineer, or just want to understand the machine behind your code, learning Linux is one of the most valuable skills you can invest in.

This guide is not a cheat sheet. It is a structured learning path that takes you from never having opened a terminal to being comfortable administering, scripting, and securing Linux systems.

Chapter 1: Choosing Your Linux Distribution

Before you type a single command, you need to pick a distribution. This choice matters less than people think — the core skills transfer across all of them — but starting with the right one saves headaches.

For beginners: Ubuntu or Linux Mint. Ubuntu has the largest community, the most tutorials written for it, and excellent hardware support. Linux Mint is based on Ubuntu and offers a more traditional desktop experience. Both use the APT package manager and the Debian packaging system.

For server work: Debian or Rocky Linux (formerly CentOS). Debian is rock-stable and uses the same package manager as Ubuntu. Rocky Linux mirrors Red Hat Enterprise Linux and uses DNF/YUM with RPM packages. Learning both Debian-based and RPM-based systems makes you versatile.

For security and penetration testing: Kali Linux or Parrot OS. Both come pre-loaded with security tools. Kali is the industry standard for penetration testing. Parrot is lighter and includes privacy tools alongside security tools.

For advanced users: Arch Linux or Gentoo. These teach you Linux from the ground up because you build everything yourself. Arch uses a rolling release model and the Pacman package manager. Gentoo compiles everything from source. Both are not for beginners, but the learning experience is unmatched.

How to install: Start with a virtual machine using VirtualBox or VMware. Download the ISO, create a VM with 2-4GB RAM and 40GB disk, and install. This gives you a safe environment to break things. Once comfortable, dual-boot or install on a dedicated machine.

Chapter 2: The Terminal — Your New Best Friend

The terminal is not something to fear. It is the most powerful interface on the system, and once you are comfortable with it, you will be faster than any GUI user.

Understanding the Shell

When you open a terminal, you are interacting with a shell. The default on most modern systems is Bash (Bourne Again Shell). Other shells include Zsh (popular for its completions and themes), Fish (user-friendly with autosuggestions), and Dash (used for system scripts on Debian/Ubuntu).

You can check your current shell with: echo $SHELL

Switch shells with: chsh -s /bin/zsh

Basic Navigation

These are the first commands to internalize:

  • pwd — Print Working Directory. Shows where you are right now.
  • ls — List directory contents. Use ls -la for detailed view including hidden files.
  • cd — Change Directory. cd .. goes up one level, cd ~ goes to your home, cd - toggles between current and previous directory.
  • mkdir — Make Directory. Use mkdir -p to create nested directories in one shot.
  • rmdir — Remove empty directories.
  • rm -r — Remove directories and their contents. Use with extreme caution. There is no trash can.
  • cp — Copy files. cp -r copies directories recursively.
  • mv — Move or rename files. mv oldname newname renames. mv file /path/ moves.
  • touch — Create an empty file or update a file timestamp.

Reading Files

  • cat — Print entire file contents to the terminal. Good for short files.
  • less — Paginated file viewer. Use arrow keys to scroll, q to quit. Better than cat for long files.
  • head — Show first N lines of a file. head -n 20 file shows first 20 lines.
  • tail — Show last N lines. tail -f /var/log/syslog follows a log file in real time.
  • nano — Simple terminal text editor. Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to exit. Good for beginners.
  • vim — Powerful but steep learning curve. Start with vimtutor to learn the basics.

Getting Help

Every command has a manual. Use man command to read it. For a quick summary, use command --help. For searching what a command does, use apropos keyword or whatis command.

Chapter 3: The Linux File System Hierarchy

Linux does not use drive letters like Windows. Everything is mounted in a single unified directory tree starting from /. Understanding this hierarchy is essential.

  • / — The root of the entire file system.
  • /home — User home directories. Your personal files go here.
  • /root — The root user home directory. Separate from /home.
  • /etc — System configuration files. Almost every service stores its config here.
  • /var — Variable data. Logs (/var/log), mail, spool files, and databases.
  • /tmp — Temporary files. Cleared on reboot. World-writable by default (sticky bit prevents deletion of others files).
  • /usr — User programs and data. /usr/bin has most commands, /usr/lib has libraries, /usr/share has documentation.
  • /bin — Essential binaries needed for boot and single-user mode.
  • /sbin — System binaries, typically for administration (iptables, fdisk, reboot).
  • /boot — Boot loader files, kernel images.
  • /dev — Device files. /dev/sda is your first disk, /dev/null is the black hole, /dev/zero provides infinite zeros.
  • /proc — Virtual file system for process and kernel information. /proc/cpuinfo, /proc/meminfo, /proc/[pid]/ are invaluable for debugging.
  • /sys — Virtual file system for device and driver information.
  • /opt — Optional software packages, typically third-party applications.
  • /srv — Data served by the system (web server content, FTP files).
  • /media — Mount points for removable media (USB drives, CD-ROMs).
  • /mnt — Temporary mount points for manual mounting.

Key insight: In Linux, everything is a file. Directories are files. Hard drives are files in /dev. Network connections appear in /proc/net. Even running processes have entries in /proc/[pid]. This uniformity is what makes Linux so powerful and scriptable.

Chapter 4: File Permissions and Ownership

This is where many beginners get confused, and for good reason — the system is powerful but not intuitive at first glance.

Understanding the Permission String

Run ls -la and you will see something like: -rwxr-xr-- 1 user group 4096 Aug 20 10:00 script.sh

Breaking it down:

  • - = file type (- for file, d for directory, l for symlink)
  • rwx = owner permissions (read, write, execute)
  • r-x = group permissions (read, execute, no write)
  • r-- = others permissions (read only)

Changing Permissions with chmod

Symbolic mode: chmod u+x file (add execute for user/owner). chmod g-w file (remove write for group). chmod o=r file (set others to read only).

Numeric mode: Each permission has a number. Read=4, Write=2, Execute=1. Add them up per scope. chmod 755 file means owner gets 7 (4+2+1), group gets 5 (4+0+1), others get 5 (4+0+1). Common values: 644 for files, 755 for directories, 700 for private directories.

Changing Ownership with chown

chown user:group file changes both owner and group. chown -R user:group /path changes recursively. You need root or sudo for this.

Special Permissions

SUID (chmod u+s): Runs the file as the file owner, not the executing user. Used by passwd to allow users to change their password which requires writing to /etc/shadow.

SGID (chmod g+s): On files, runs with the group privileges. On directories, new files inherit the directory group. Useful for shared project directories.

Sticky bit (chmod +t): On directories, only the file owner can delete their own files, even if others have write permission. Used on /tmp.

Chapter 5: Users and Groups

Linux is a multi-user system. Understanding user management is fundamental.

Essential Commands

  • whoami — Shows your current username.
  • id — Shows your UID, GID, and group memberships.
  • who — Shows who is currently logged in.
  • su - username — Switch to another user. su - alone switches to root.
  • sudo command — Execute a command as root (or another user). The proper way to escalate privileges.

Managing Users

  • useradd -m username — Create a user with a home directory.
  • passwd username — Set or change a user password.
  • usermod -aG groupname username — Add a user to a group. The -a flag appends (without it, the user is removed from all other groups).
  • userdel -r username — Delete a user and their home directory.

Managing Groups

  • groupadd groupname — Create a new group.
  • groupdel groupname — Delete a group.
  • groups username — Show which groups a user belongs to.

The sudo System

The /etc/sudoers file controls who can run what as root. Never edit this file directly — use visudo which validates syntax before saving. A typical entry: username ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL allows a user to run any command. username ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL allows passwordless sudo (use sparingly).

The /etc/sudoers.d/ directory allows dropping in per-user or per-group config files without touching the main file.

Chapter 6: Package Management

Installing, updating, and removing software is a daily task. The commands differ between distributions.

Debian/Ubuntu (APT)

  • apt update — Refresh package lists from repositories.
  • apt upgrade — Upgrade all installed packages.
  • apt install package — Install a package.
  • apt remove package — Remove a package (keep config).
  • apt purge package — Remove a package and its config files.
  • apt search keyword — Search for packages.
  • apt show package — Show package details.
  • dpkg -l — List all installed packages.
  • dpkg -L package — List files installed by a package.

RHEL/CentOS/Rocky (DNF/YUM)

  • dnf check-update — Check for updates.
  • dnf update — Update all packages.
  • dnf install package — Install a package.
  • dnf remove package — Remove a package.
  • dnf search keyword — Search for packages.
  • rpm -qa — List all installed RPM packages.

Arch (Pacman)

  • pacman -Syu — Full system upgrade.
  • pacman -S package — Install a package.
  • pacman -R package — Remove a package.
  • pacman -Ss keyword — Search for packages.

Universal Package Formats

Flatpak and Snap are distribution-agnostic package formats. Flatpak uses flathub.org as its main repository. Snap uses the snap store. Both sandbox applications and work across distributions. Install with: flatpak install package or snap install package.

Chapter 7: Process Management

Understanding and controlling running processes is critical for system administration.

Viewing Processes

  • ps aux — Show all running processes with detailed information. The classic command.
  • ps aux | grep processname — Filter for a specific process.
  • top — Real-time process monitor. Shows CPU, memory, and process count. Press q to quit, M to sort by memory, P to sort by CPU.
  • htop — Enhanced version of top with color, mouse support, and tree view. Install with: apt install htop.
  • pstree — Show processes as a tree. Great for understanding parent-child relationships.

Controlling Processes

  • Ctrl+C — Send SIGINT (interrupt) to the foreground process. Stops most commands.
  • Ctrl+Z — Send SIGTSTP (suspend) to the foreground process. Use fg to resume or bg to run in background.
  • kill PID — Send SIGTERM (graceful termination) to a process.
  • kill -9 PID — Send SIGKILL (forced termination). Use only when SIGTERM fails.
  • killall processname — Kill all instances of a process by name.
  • pkill processname — Kill processes matching a pattern.
  • nohup command & — Run a command that survives terminal closure.

Process Priority

Use nice and renice to control process scheduling priority. nice -n 10 command starts a command with lower priority (nice value 10). renice -n -5 -p PID changes the priority of a running process. Values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest).

Systemd and Services

Most modern Linux systems use systemd to manage services (daemons):

  • systemctl status service — Check if a service is running.
  • systemctl start service — Start a service.
  • systemctl stop service — Stop a service.
  • systemctl restart service — Restart a service.
  • systemctl enable service — Auto-start a service on boot.
  • systemctl disable service — Prevent a service from starting on boot.
  • journalctl -u service — View logs for a service.

Chapter 8: Disk Management and Storage

Managing disks, partitions, and file systems is a core sysadmin skill.

Disk Information

  • lsblk — List block devices (disks and partitions) in a tree view. The most useful command for disk overview.
  • fdisk -l — List all disks and partitions with detailed information.
  • df -h — Show disk space usage by mounted file systems. The -h flag makes it human-readable.
  • du -sh /path — Show the size of a directory. du -sh * in a directory shows the size of each item.

Partitioning

Use fdisk for MBR (legacy) or gdisk/parted for GPT (modern). For most use cases: parted /dev/sdb is the easiest interactive tool. Create a partition table (gpt or msdos), then create partitions with specified size and type.

File Systems

mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1 creates an ext4 file system. mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb1 creates XFS. ext4 is the most common general-purpose file system. XFS is better for large files and high-performance workloads. btrfs offers snapshots, compression, and checksums — increasingly popular for root file systems.

Mounting

mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data mounts a partition to a directory. umount /mnt/data unmounts it. For permanent mounts, add entries to /etc/fstab. Format: UUID=uuid /mountpoint filesystem defaults 0 0. Use UUIDs instead of device names as they are more reliable across reboots.

LVM (Logical Volume Manager)

LVM allows flexible disk management — resize volumes, add disks to existing volumes, and create snapshots. The hierarchy is: Physical Volumes (PV) -> Volume Groups (VG) -> Logical Volumes (LV). Learn pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, and lvextend as your starting commands.

Chapter 9: Networking

Linux networking is deep, but these fundamentals will get you through most situations.

Network Information

  • ip addr — Show IP addresses and interfaces. Replaces the old ifconfig command.
  • ip link — Show network interfaces and their state (up/down).
  • ip route — Show the routing table. Replaces route command.
  • ss -tlnp — Show listening TCP sockets with process information. Replaces netstat.
  • ss -anp — Show all sockets with process info.
  • cat /etc/resolv.conf — Show DNS resolver configuration.

Testing Connectivity

  • ping host — Test basic network connectivity. ping -c 4 host sends exactly 4 packets.
  • traceroute host — Show the path packets take to a host. Shows each router hop.
  • dig domain — DNS lookup. More detailed than nslookup. dig domain AAAA shows IPv6 records.
  • nslookup domain — Simple DNS lookup.
  • curl -I https://example.com — Fetch HTTP headers from a URL. Useful for testing web servers.
  • wget url — Download a file from a URL.

Network Configuration

On Ubuntu, network configuration lives in /etc/netplan/ as YAML files. On RHEL/Rocky, it is in /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ or managed by NetworkManager. nmcli is the command-line tool for NetworkManager: nmcli device status shows interface states, nmcli connection show lists configured connections.

Firewalls

UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) is the beginner-friendly frontend on Ubuntu: ufw enable, ufw allow 22/tcp, ufw allow 80/tcp, ufw status. For more control, use iptables directly or nftables on modern systems. firewalld is the default on RHEL/CentOS with zone-based configuration.

SSH

ssh user@host connects to a remote machine. ssh-keygen -t ed25519 generates a key pair. ssh-copy-id user@host installs your public key on the remote server for passwordless login. ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@host creates a local port tunnel. ssh -D 1080 user@host creates a SOCKS proxy.

Chapter 10: Shell Scripting

Shell scripting is what turns a Linux user into a Linux power user. It automates repetitive tasks and chains commands together.

Your First Script

Create a file called hello.sh:

#!/bin/bash
echo 'Hello from Linux!'
echo 'Today is' $(date)
echo 'You are running as' $(whoami)

Make it executable: chmod +x hello.sh. Run it: ./hello.sh.

Variables

NAME='Linux' echo $NAME stores and uses a variable. Use $(command) for command substitution. Use ${VARIABLE} for clarity in strings. Quote strings with spaces: MESSAGE='Hello World' echo $MESSAGE.

Conditionals

if [ condition ]; then commands; fi. Test with: -f file (exists and is regular file), -d dir (exists and is directory), -z string (string is empty), -n string (string is not empty), string1 = string2 (strings are equal), -eq -ne -lt -gt -le -ge (numeric comparisons).

Loops

for file in *.log; do echo $file; done loops over files. for i in $(seq 1 10); do echo $i; done loops over a range. while read line; do echo $line; done file reads a file line by line.

Functions

function greet { echo Hello $1; } greet World defines and calls a function. $1 is the first argument, $2 is the second, $@ is all arguments.

Useful Patterns

Error handling: set -e stops on first error, set -u treats unset variables as errors, set -o pipefail catches pipe failures. Use these at the top of every serious script. Logging: redirect output to a log file with exec > /var/log/myscript.log 2>&1. Check command success with: if command; then echo success; else echo failed; fi.

Practical Script Examples

Backup script: Use tar to archive a directory with a timestamp in the filename, then optionally upload to remote storage. System monitoring script: Parse df, free, and uptime commands, check thresholds, and send alerts via email or webhook. Log rotation script: Find old log files, compress them, and delete beyond a retention period.

Chapter 11: Text Processing and Pipelines

Linux is built around text processing. Mastering these tools unlocks incredible productivity.

grep — Search Text

grep pattern file searches for a pattern in a file. grep -r pattern /path searches recursively. grep -i pattern ignores case. grep -v pattern inverts the match. grep -c pattern counts matches. grep -n pattern shows line numbers. grep -E uses extended regex for complex patterns.

sed — Stream Editor

sed 's/old/new/g' file replaces text. sed -n '10,20p' file prints lines 10-20. sed -i 's/old/new/g' file edits the file in place. sed '/pattern/d' file deletes matching lines. sed '3a new line' file inserts a line after line 3.

awk — Text Processing

awk '{print $1}' file prints the first field of each line. awk -F: '{print $1, $3}' /etc/passwd uses colon as delimiter and prints username and UID. awk '$3 > 1000' file filters lines where the third field is greater than 1000. awk '{sum += $1} END {print sum}' file calculates a sum.

Pipes and Redirection

The pipe operator | sends the output of one command as input to the next. cat file | grep pattern | wc -l counts lines matching a pattern. Use > to redirect output to a file (overwrites), >> to append, 2> to redirect errors, and 2>&1 to redirect errors to the same place as output. /dev/null is the black hole — discard anything you send there.

sort, uniq, cut, tr

sort file sorts lines. sort -u file sorts and removes duplicates. uniq -c counts consecutive duplicates (pipe through sort first). cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd cuts by delimiter and field. tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' translates lowercase to uppercase. tr -d ' ' removes carriage returns.

Chapter 12: System Monitoring and Troubleshooting

When something goes wrong, knowing where to look saves hours of frustration.

System Logs

/var/log/syslog (or /var/log/messages on RHEL) contains general system logs. /var/log/auth.log (or /var/log/secure) has authentication events. /var/log/kern.log has kernel messages. Use journalctl for systemd-based systems: journalctl -f follows logs, journalctl -u service shows service logs, journalctl --since '1 hour ago' filters by time.

Performance Monitoring

uptime shows load averages. free -h shows memory usage. vmstat 1 shows virtual memory statistics every second. iostat 1 shows disk I/O statistics. sar collects and reports system activity. nmon combines multiple metrics in one view.

Common Troubleshooting Steps

  • System running slow? Check load average with uptime, check memory with free -h, check disk I/O with iostat, check top processes with top or htop.
  • Service not starting? Check status with systemctl status, check logs with journalctl, check config with the service-specific tool.
  • Network not working? Check interfaces with ip addr, check routes with ip route, test connectivity with ping, check DNS with dig, check firewall with ufw status or iptables -L.
  • Disk full? Run df -h to find which partition, then du -sh /* to find the large directories, drill down until you find the culprit.

Chapter 13: Security Fundamentals

Security is not optional. Even on a personal machine, these practices matter.

Users and Authentication

Never use root for daily work. Use sudo for privilege escalation. Set strong passwords with complexity requirements. Implement SSH key authentication and disable password login. Use PAM modules for advanced authentication policies.

File System Security

Set proper permissions — least privilege principle. Use chattr +i to make critical files immutable (even root cannot modify without removing the flag first). Use acl for fine-grained access control. Mount partitions with noexec, nosuid, and nodev where appropriate.

Network Security

Configure firewalls to deny all by default and allow only necessary ports. Use fail2ban to block brute-force attempts. Implement fail2ban for SSH, web applications, and any login-facing service. Monitor /var/log/auth.log for suspicious activity.

Encryption

Use LUKS for full disk encryption. Use GPG for file and email encryption. Use SSH for all remote access. Use TLS/HTTPS for all web traffic. Store secrets in encrypted vaults, not in plain text files.

Auditing

Install and configure auditd to track system calls and file access. Use Lynis for automated security auditing of your system. Run rkhunter and chkrootkit regularly to detect rootkits. Monitor for unexpected SUID/SGID binaries.

Chapter 14: Virtualization and Containers

Modern infrastructure runs on virtualization and containers. Linux is the foundation for both.

KVM/QEMU

KVM is the kernel-based virtual machine built into Linux. Combined with QEMU for hardware emulation, it provides full virtualization. Manage with virsh command: virsh list --all shows all VMs, virsh start name starts a VM, virsh console name connects to a VM console.

Docker

Docker packages applications in containers. docker pull image downloads an image, docker run -it image bash starts an interactive container, docker ps shows running containers, docker exec -it container bash runs a command in a running container. Learn to write Dockerfiles to build custom images.

Podman

Podman is a daemonless container engine compatible with Docker but runs containers as individual processes without a central daemon. It supports rootless containers by default, making it more secure. The CLI is almost identical to Docker.

Chapter 15: Learning Resources and Practice

Theory without practice is useless. Here is how to actually learn.

Free Resources

  • Linux Journey (linuxjourney.com) — Excellent interactive beginner guide.
  • The Linux Command Line (linuxcommand.org) — Free comprehensive book by William Shotts.
  • OverTheWire Bandit — Learn Linux basics through a wargame. Perfect for hands-on practice.
  • HackTheBox and TryHackMe — Practice Linux in realistic security scenarios.
  • Linux From Scratch (linuxfromscratch.org) — Build your own Linux system from source. Advanced but educational.

Practice Environments

Set up a home lab with VirtualBox or VMware. Create VMs with different distributions. Break things on purpose and fix them. Set up a web server, database, and application stack. Configure networking between VMs. Simulate failures and troubleshoot them.

Use cloud free tiers (Oracle Cloud always-free, AWS free tier, Google Cloud free tier) to practice on real servers. A cheap VPS from Hetzner or Contabo gives you a real Linux environment to administer.

The Learning Path

Week 1-2: Install a distribution, learn navigation, basic commands, file operations. Week 3-4: Permissions, users, groups, package management. Week 5-6: Processes, services, disk management. Week 7-8: Networking basics, SSH, firewall configuration. Week 9-10: Shell scripting fundamentals. Week 11-12: Text processing, system monitoring, log analysis. Week 13-14: Security hardening, basic forensics. Week 15-16: Containers, virtualization, automation.

After this foundation, specialize based on your career goals: cloud engineering, security, DevOps, or embedded systems.

Conclusion

Learning Linux is a marathon, not a sprint. The command line will feel awkward at first. You will forget flags and syntax. You will accidentally delete something important. Every Linux professional has been there. The key is consistency — spend at least 30 minutes daily in a terminal, work on real projects, and do not be afraid to break things in a safe environment.

The skills you build here transfer to every domain of technology. Linux knowledge makes you a better developer, a better security professional, and a better engineer. The terminal is not just a tool — it is a mindset. Once you think in pipelines and processes, you will see computing differently forever.

title: Linux File Permissions: A Deep Dive Beyond chmod 777
excerpt: Understanding UID/GID, sticky bits, ACLs, and why blindly setting 777 permissions is a security disaster waiting to happen.
content:
We have all seen it — a developer stuck on a permission error, and someone says just run chmod 777. It works, but it is the equivalent of leaving your front door wide open because you lost your keys. Let us talk about how Linux permissions actually work and why understanding them matters.

Traditional UNIX Permissions

Every file and directory in Linux has an owner, a group, and a set of permissions split into three categories: read (r), write (w), and execute (x). These apply to three scopes: the owner, the group, and everyone else.

When you run ls -la, the first column shows these permissions as a string like -rwxr-xr--. The first character indicates file type — a dash means regular file, d means directory, l means symbolic link. The next three are owner permissions, the next three are group, and the last three are for others.

Numeric representation maps directly: r=4, w=2, x=1. So rwx is 7 (4+2+1), r-x is 5 (4+0+1), and r-- is 4 (4+0+0). When you see chmod 755, the owner gets rwx (7), the group gets r-x (5), and others get r-x (5).

Why 777 Is Dangerous

chmod 777 gives read, write, and execute permissions to everyone. On a web server, this means any user on the system can modify your application files, plant malicious scripts, or read sensitive configuration files containing database credentials.

Consider a real scenario: a WordPress site has wp-config.php set to 777. Any local user on the server — including service accounts for unrelated applications — can read the database password, connect to MySQL, and dump your entire customer database. They can also inject PHP backdoors into your theme files that execute with the web server privileges.

A more secure approach for web files: chmod 644 for files and chmod 755 for directories. The web server user (www-data) should be added to the file group rather than making files world-writable. For sensitive files like .env and wp-config.php, use chmod 600 so only the owner can read them.

Understanding umask

The umask determines the default permissions for new files and directories. A umask of 022 means new files get 644 (666 minus 022) and directories get 755 (777 minus 022). For a more secure default, set umask 027 in /etc/profile — this makes new files 640 and directories 750, keeping group members out of files they do not need access to.

Check your current umask by running umask with no arguments. If it returns 0000, your system is creating world-readable files by default, which is a security problem on multi-user systems.

The Sticky Bit, SUID, and SGID

Linux has special permission bits that go beyond the basic rwx model:

  • Sticky bit: On directories like /tmp, this prevents users from deleting files they do not own. Without it, any user could delete another user temporary files. Set it with chmod +t /path/to/dir or chmod 1777 /path/to/dir.
  • SUID (Set User ID): Runs the file with the owner privileges. The passwd command uses SUID so regular users can update their password hash in /etc/shadow, which is only writable by root. Set it with chmod u+s /path/to/binary or chmod 4755.
  • SGID (Set Group ID): On executables, runs with the group privileges. On directories, new files inherit the directory group instead of the creating user primary group. This is useful for shared project directories where all files need to belong to the same group.

Find SUID Binaries on Your System

A common privilege escalation technique involves finding misconfigured SUID binaries. Audit your system with: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null

Common abusable SUID binaries include nmap (interactive mode runs shell), vim (:shell command), find (-exec flag), python (import os; os.execl('/bin/sh','sh','-p')), and bash (bash -p gives root shell). If you find any of these with SUID bit set, remove the SUID immediately with chmod u-s.

Also check for SGID binaries: find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null. While less commonly exploited, SGID binaries on directories can be used for group-based escalation.

Access Control Lists

When traditional permissions are not granular enough, ACLs let you set permissions for specific users or groups without changing ownership. This is essential when you need to give one specific user access to a file without adding them to the file group.

View ACLs with getfacl /path/to/file. Set them with setfacl -m u:username:rwx /path/to/file. Remove them with setfacl -x u:username /path/to/file. ACLs show up as a + in ls -la output.

For directories, set default ACLs so new files automatically inherit the right permissions: setfacl -d -m u:username:rwx /path/to/dir. This solves the common problem of giving someone access to existing files but not to files they create later.

Ownership and Group Management

Changing ownership is sometimes necessary but should be done carefully. chown user:group /path/to/file changes both owner and group. chown -R user:group /path/to/dir changes recursively.

Never chown -R root:root on a web application directory — the web server needs to write to uploads, cache, and log directories. Instead, identify which specific directories need write access and set ownership on those individually.

For shared directories, create a dedicated group (groupadd devteam), add users to it (usermod -aG devteam username), and set the directory with SGID so all new files inherit the group: chown :devteam /shared && chmod 2775 /shared.

Practical Hardening Steps

Audit SUID and SGID binaries regularly with find / -perm /6000 -type f 2>/dev/null. Remove unnecessary SUID bits — most do not need them. Use ACLs instead of group-wide permissions for fine-grained access. Mount partitions with nosuid and noexec where possible, especially /tmp, /var/tmp, and /dev/shm.

Use umask 027 to ensure new files are never world-readable by default. Monitor permission changes with auditd: auditctl -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes. This logs every write or attribute change to /etc/passwd, alerting you if someone adds a new user or changes ownership.

For web servers, the principle of least privilege applies directly: the web server process should run as a dedicated user (www-data), have read access only to application code, write access only to uploads and cache directories, and no access to database credentials outside the application config.

title: From iptables to nftables: Building a Production Firewall on Linux
excerpt: A practical guide to configuring stateful packet filtering, NAT, rate limiting, and migrating legacy iptables rules to the modern nftables framework.
content:
Every Linux server needs a firewall. Whether you are running a single VPS or a cluster of containers, understanding packet filtering at the kernel level is non-negotiable for anyone serious about security.

iptables: The Legacy That Won't Die

iptables has been the default Linux firewall for over two decades. It uses the Netfilter framework to hook into the kernel networking stack. The rules are organized into chains within tables. The four primary tables are filter (default filtering), nat (address translation), mangle (packet modification), and raw (connection tracking bypass).

Each table has built-in chains: INPUT for traffic destined to the host, OUTPUT for traffic originating from the host, FORWARD for traffic passing through (routers), PREROUTING for traffic arriving at the network interface, and POSTROUTING for traffic leaving the interface.

A basic iptables setup drops all incoming traffic by default, allows loopback, permits established connections, and opens SSH and HTTPS:

iptables -P INPUT DROP
iptables -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT

The -P flag sets the default policy. The -A flag appends a rule to a chain. The -m flag loads a match extension like conntrack for stateful inspection. Rules are evaluated top to bottom, and the first match wins.

Persistent rules require saving with iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4 and restoring on boot with iptables-restore. On Debian systems, install iptables-persistent to automate this. On RHEL systems, use service iptables save.

Why nftables Is the Future

nftables replaced iptables starting with Linux kernel 3.13 and is now the default on most distributions. It provides a single unified framework instead of the fragmented table and chain model. The syntax is cleaner, performance is better with large rule sets (especially when dealing with thousands of rules), and it supports set-based matching for efficient rule evaluation.

Key advantages over iptables: atomic rule replacement (no race conditions during updates), native IPv6 support in the same ruleset, built-in set types for IP lists and port ranges, automatic rule reordering, and better logging with built-in counters and quotas.

nftables uses a single command-line tool (nft) instead of the separate iptables, ip6tables, arptables, and ebtables commands. Rules are organized in tables and chains like iptables, but the syntax is more consistent and readable.

Practical nftables Configuration

Here is a production-ready nftables config for a web server that drops invalid packets, allows loopback and established connections, opens SSH and HTTPS, blocks known bad IPs, and rate limits ICMP. Save this to /etc/nftables.conf and enable with systemctl enable nftables.

The configuration uses the inet family (which handles both IPv4 and IPv6), sets a default drop policy, accepts established connections, allows loopback traffic, opens required ports, rate limits ICMP echo requests, and logs dropped packets with a prefix for analysis. This single ruleset handles both address families, which is simpler than maintaining separate iptables and ip6tables configurations.

For a Docker host, add additional rules for the docker0 bridge interface and containers. The FORWARD chain needs to accept traffic on docker0 and br- interfaces while still blocking unauthorized access to the host itself.

Rate Limiting and Anti-DDoS

Raw packet rate limiting in nftables can mitigate basic volumetric attacks. The limit statement combined with burst controls how many packets per second a rule will match. For SYN flood protection, use connection tracking with aggressive timeouts and drop invalid packets early.

For more advanced protection, combine nftables with fail2ban for application-level banning. The nftables integration in fail2ban allows automatic IP blacklisting after repeated failed login attempts. Create a blacklist set with timeout entries that automatically expire after a configurable period.

For distributed attacks, consider using nftables sets with timeout entries that automatically expire. Add elements to the blacklist set with a timeout, and nftables will automatically remove them when the timeout expires. This is more efficient than managing individual rules for temporary bans.

NAT and Port Forwarding

nftables handles NAT through a separate ip nat table. For port forwarding a public port to an internal container, use the prerouting chain with a DNAT target. The postrouting chain handles masquerading for outbound traffic from containers.

For hairpin NAT (accessing a container from the same host using its public IP), add an additional rule in the prerouting chain that matches on the host IP address. This is common in Docker and Kubernetes environments where services need to reach other services on the same host through the published port.

Source NAT (SNAT) is used when you want to change the source IP of outgoing traffic. This is useful when a server has multiple public IPs and you want outbound traffic to use a specific IP. Masquerading is a special case of SNAT that automatically uses the IP of the outgoing interface.

Migration Tips

Convert existing iptables rules using iptables-save piped to nft. The conversion is not always perfect for complex rule sets with custom chains and non-standard matches, so test thoroughly. Tools like iptables-translate can convert individual rules to nftables syntax.

For gradual migration, run both iptables and nftables simultaneously during the transition period. nftables and iptables use different Netfilter hooks, so they do not conflict. Once you have verified the nftables rules work correctly, remove the old iptables rules.

Always keep a backup of your working firewall configuration before making changes. Use nft -f /etc/nftables.conf to reload the entire ruleset atomically, or make incremental changes with nft add and nft delete commands. Test from a separate session to avoid locking yourself out.

title: Common Linux Privilege Escalation Vectors You Should Know
excerpt: From SUID misconfigurations to kernel exploits — understanding how attackers escalate privileges helps you defend against it.
content:
Getting a low-privilege shell on a Linux system is often just the beginning. Understanding privilege escalation techniques is essential for both offensive security professionals and defenders who need to know what to harden.

Sudo Misconfigurations

The most common escalation path. Run sudo -l to see what commands your user can execute as root. Look for NOPASSWD entries, wildcard entries, and scripts that call other binaries without absolute paths which enables PATH manipulation attacks.

The GTFOBins database is the definitive reference for abusing legitimate binaries for privilege escalation. Common entries include vim with :!sh, find with -exec, python with os module, bash with -p flag, and env with /bin/sh.

Another common misconfiguration: the user can run a specific script as root, but that script calls another binary without an absolute path. You can create a fake binary in /tmp, prepend /tmp to PATH, and when the script runs, it executes your malicious version instead. Always audit sudo configurations with visudo to validate syntax.

SUID and SGID Binaries

Find all SUID binaries with: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null. Also search for SGID: find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null. And for binaries with both: find / -perm -6000 -type f 2>/dev/null.

Common abusable SUID binaries include nmap in interactive mode (old versions), vim with :shell command, find with -exec flag, python with os module to spawn shell, bash with -p flag to preserve effective UID, env with /bin/sh, awk with system(), and perl with -e exec.

If you find a custom SUID binary (not a standard system binary), run strings on it to look for hardcoded paths, file operations, or command executions that might be exploitable. Check if it reads from a writable location or writes to a predictable path. Use ltrace and strace to observe its behavior at runtime.

Cron Jobs

Check /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, /etc/cron.daily/, /etc/cron.hourly/, /etc/cron.weekly/, and /var/spool/cron/ for scheduled tasks. Look for scripts running as root that your user can modify, wildcards in cron commands, and cron jobs running scripts in writable directories.

A common pattern: a root cron job runs /opt/backup.sh every hour. If you can write to /opt/backup.sh, you can add a reverse shell command that executes on the next cron run. Even if the script is not writable, check if the directory is writable and the cron job uses a wildcard. Tar with * can be exploited with --checkpoint-action flags that execute arbitrary commands.

Kernel Exploits

Check the kernel version with uname -a and search for known exploits. Notable ones include DirtyPipe (CVE-2022-0847, affects kernels 5.8 to 5.16.11), DirtyCow (CVE-2016-5195, affects kernels 2.6.22 to 4.8.3), and PwnKit for polkit (CVE-2021-4034, affects most systems with polkit installed).

Always check if patches are available before considering kernel exploits. Running an unpatched kernel exploit on a production system can cause data corruption or system instability. Check with apt list --installed | grep linux-image and compare against available security updates. The uname -r command shows the exact kernel version including the distribution-specific suffix.

Capabilities

Linux capabilities break root privileges into discrete units. Check with getcap -r / 2>/dev/null. A binary with cap_setuid can escalate to root. Python with cap_setuid gives you root immediately by calling os.setuid(0) and then spawning a shell.

Common dangerous capabilities: cap_setuid (set user ID), cap_setgid (set group ID), cap_dac_override (bypass file permission checks), cap_sys_admin (various system administration operations), cap_net_raw (raw socket access for sniffing), and cap_sys_ptrace (trace and inspect other processes).

Capabilities can be set with setcap: setcap cap_setuid+ep /usr/bin/python3 gives Python the ability to set its own UID. This is often overlooked in security audits because traditional focus is on SUID bits rather than capabilities.

World-Writable Paths and Misconfigurations

Directories with 777 permissions in system paths can be exploited by planting malicious scripts. Check /etc, /usr/local/bin, /opt, and application directories. Also check for readable /etc/shadow (use unshadow to combine with /etc/passwd for offline cracking), writable /etc/passwd (add a new root user), and exposed environment variables containing credentials in /proc/*/environ.

SSH keys in known locations are another vector. Check ~/.ssh/ for authorized_keys entries you can modify, and /root/.ssh/ if you can read it. If authorized_keys is writable, you can add your own public key and SSH as root. Also check for world-readable private keys with: find / -name id_rsa -o -name id_ed25519 2>/dev/null.

Defense Checklist

Audit sudo -l for all users regularly. Remove unnecessary SUID bits with chmod u-s. Keep kernels patched and subscribe to security mailing lists for your distribution. Use nosuid mount option where possible on /tmp, /var/tmp, and /dev/shm. Monitor with auditd for suspicious execve calls that indicate privilege escalation attempts.

Implement least-privilege principles across all service accounts. Shell scripts called by root should use absolute paths for all binaries. Review cron jobs weekly and remove entries that are no longer needed. Regularly check for world-writable files and directories with: find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 2>/dev/null.

title: Hardening Your SSH Server: A Step-by-Step Security Guide
excerpt: SSH is the most common attack surface on Linux servers. Here is how to lock it down properly.
content:
SSH is the front door to your server. Default configurations are designed for compatibility, not security. Every hardened server should start with SSH hardening.

Disable Root Login

In /etc/ssh/sshd_config, set PermitRootLogin no. This forces attackers to guess both a username and password. Always use a regular user account and escalate with sudo. If you need to run commands as root, configure sudo properly rather than logging in directly as root.

For automated deployments, create a dedicated deploy user with limited sudo permissions for specific commands, rather than using root directly. This gives you an audit trail and limits the blast radius if the deploy key is compromised. Use a restricted shell for the deploy user if possible.

Switch to Key-Based Authentication

Password authentication should be disabled entirely. Generate a key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100. Ed25519 is faster, more secure, and produces smaller keys than RSA. If you need RSA for legacy systems, use at least 4096 bits.

Copy the public key to the server with ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@server. After verifying key-based login works, disable PasswordAuthentication, ChallengeResponseAuthentication, and UsePAM in sshd_config.

Protect your private key with a strong passphrase. Store it in ~/.ssh/ with permissions 600 (chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519). Never share private keys between machines or users. Use ssh-agent to cache the passphrase during your session rather than leaving the key unencrypted. Add the key to the agent with ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.

Change the Default Port

Changing from port 22 does not stop a determined attacker, but it eliminates 99 percent of automated brute-force attempts that scan only port 22. Choose a port above 1024 to avoid conflicts and log it somewhere accessible so you remember it.

Update your SSH client config (~/.ssh/config) to remember the new port. This way you do not need to type the port every time. Also update your firewall rules to open the new port and close port 22 after verifying the new port works.

Limit User Access

Only allow specific users to connect with AllowUsers or AllowGroups directives. This prevents compromised service accounts from being used as entry points. For example, AllowUsers deploy admin limits SSH access to only those two accounts.

For team environments, use AllowGroups and create a dedicated ssh-users group. Add users to this group when they need SSH access and remove them when they do not. This is easier to manage than maintaining a list of individual users. DenyGroups is also available for explicit denials.

Connection Limits and Timeouts

Set MaxAuthTries to 3 to prevent brute-force attempts. Set LoginGraceTime to 30 seconds so unauthenticated connections are dropped quickly. Configure ClientAliveInterval 300 and ClientAliveCountMax 2 to disconnect idle sessions after 10 minutes.

For additional protection, set MaxSessions to 10 to limit concurrent sessions per connection, and MaxStartups 10:30:60 to limit unauthenticated connections. The format is start:rate:full where start is the number of unauthenticated connections before rate limiting kicks in, rate is the probability of dropping (out of 128), and full is the number where all new connections are dropped.

Disable Unnecessary Features

Turn off X11Forwarding, AllowTcpForwarding, AllowAgentForwarding, and PermitTunnel unless you specifically need them. Each feature you disable reduces the attack surface. If you only need direct shell access, disable everything except what is required.

If you use SSH for Git operations, you may need AllowTcpForwarding for the Git protocol. In that case, restrict it to specific users with Match blocks. Match User git followed by AllowTcpForwarding yes, and set AllowTcpForwarding no globally.

Use Fail2Ban

Install and configure Fail2Ban to automatically ban IPs after repeated failed attempts. Create /etc/fail2ban/jail.local with sshd jail enabled, maxretry set to 3, bantime set to 3600 seconds, and findtime set to 600 seconds. This bans IPs for 1 hour after 3 failed attempts within 10 minutes.

Check bans with fail2ban-client status sshd. Unban IPs with fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip. For repeated offenders, increase bantime to 86400 (24 hours) or use permanent bans. Recidive jail can automatically increase bantime for repeat offenders.

SSH Configuration Hardening Summary

Here is a complete hardened sshd_config worth copying. Use a non-standard port, disable root login, enable pubkey authentication only, set aggressive connection limits, disable X11 forwarding and TCP forwarding, and restrict users to a specific allow list.

After making changes, always test with sshd -t to check config syntax. Keep a secondary session open while testing to avoid locking yourself out. Reload with systemctl reload sshd instead of restarting to maintain existing connections. The reload command sends a SIGHUP to the daemon which re-reads the config without dropping active connections.

Verify Your Configuration

After deploying the hardened config, scan from an external machine with nmap to verify the SSH version is displayed and no unexpected services are running. Use ssh -vvv to see the full negotiation and verify your settings are applied.

Check your logs regularly with journalctl -u sshd --since today. Look for failed login attempts, connection attempts from unexpected IPs, and any errors in the SSH daemon. Set up log monitoring with logwatch or a SIEM solution for automated alerts. Consider using Shorewall or firewalld integration for dynamic SSH blocking.

title: Introduction to Linux Forensics: Investigating a Compromised System
excerpt: A systematic approach to examining a Linux system after a security incident, from volatile memory to disk artifacts.
content:
When you suspect a Linux system has been compromised, how you respond in the first few minutes determines whether you can reconstruct what happened. This guide covers the essential steps of Linux forensic investigation.

Order of Volatility

Evidence collection follows the order of volatility — collect the most ephemeral data first. The general order is: CPU registers and cache (nanoseconds), RAM (minutes to hours), network state (minutes to hours), disk (days to weeks), remote logging and archives (months).

If you shut down the system before collecting volatile data, you lose evidence that cannot be recovered. RAM contains running processes, network connections, encryption keys, loaded kernel modules, and malware that only exists in memory. The decision to collect live evidence versus pulling the plug depends on what you are trying to prove and whether the attacker is actively destroying evidence.

Live Acquisition — Memory

If you can safely image memory without shutting down the system, use LiME (Linux Memory Extractor). Memory captures running processes, network connections, encryption keys, and malware that only exists in RAM. LiME creates a kernel module that captures memory to a file or network socket.

Load the LiME module with: sudo insmod lime.ko "path=/forensics/memory.lime format=lime". The format option supports lime (standard), padded, and raw formats. Padded adds a gap between memory ranges for easier analysis. Raw is a flat dump without metadata.

Analyze the memory dump with Volatility. Use linux.pslist to show running processes, linux.netstat to show network connections, linux.bash to show bash history from memory, and linux.check_syscall to detect rootkit hooks. Volatility 3 is the current version with the best Linux support.

Capturing Volatile System State

Before touching the disk, capture running processes with ps auxwwf (the w flag shows full command lines, f shows process trees), open network connections with ss -tlnp (shows PIDs), loaded kernel modules with lsmod, logged-in users with w, and cron jobs for all users.

Additional volatile data to capture: open files with lsof (shows deleted files still held open), ARP cache with arp -a, routing table with ip route, DNS cache with systemd-resolve --statistics, and kernel ring buffer with dmesg.

Redirect all output to a forensic partition or remote syslog — never write to the compromised system disk if possible. For comprehensive collection, run a live response script that captures all volatile artifacts systematically. Timestamp every output file and verify hashes.

Disk Forensics

Create a forensic image with dd or dc3dd (dd with progress and hash support). Always hash the source and destination to verify integrity. Use dc3dd if=/dev/sda hash=sha256 to create a verified image with built-in hashing.

Mount the image read-only before examination with mount -o ro,loop,noexec. Never mount read-write — even accidentally modifying a timestamp can destroy evidence. Use The Sleuth Kit for file system analysis: fls lists files (including deleted ones), ils extracts inode information, icat recovers file contents, and tsk_recover extracts deleted files.

For modern file systems like ext4 and XFS, use the sleuth kit's extundelete to recover deleted files. Check for hidden partitions, encrypted volumes, and slack space where data might be concealed.

Timeline Analysis

Build a timeline of file system activity using fls and mactime from The Sleuth Kit. This creates a chronological view of all file modifications, access times, and changes — invaluable for identifying what the attacker touched.

Generate a timeline with: fls -r -m / /forensics/disk_image.raw > bodyfile.txt && mactime -b bodyfile.txt -d > timeline.csv. The -r flag processes directories recursively, -m sets the mount point. The output CSV can be opened in a spreadsheet or analyzed with scripts.

Focus on unusual timestamps: files modified in /usr/bin or /usr/sbin suggest replaced binaries, modifications to /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow suggest user account changes, new files in /tmp or /dev/shm suggest attacker tools, and changes to cron directories suggest persistence mechanisms.

Key Artifacts to Examine

bash_history: Check all users history files including hidden ones at ~/.bash_history. Also check /root/.bash_history and /home/*/.bash_history. Attackers often forget to clear history or leave partial traces.

/var/log/auth.log: Login attempts, sudo usage, SSH connections, PAM authentication events. Look for successful logins from unusual IPs, sudo usage from non-admin users, and SSH key additions. Also check /var/log/secure on RHEL-based systems.

/var/log/syslog and /var/log/kern.log: System events, service starts and stops, kernel messages. Service restarts may indicate persistence mechanisms being activated.

/tmp and /dev/shm: Common locations for attacker tools. These directories are often mounted with noexec but attackers use Perl, Python, or bash scripts that do not need execute permission.

Web server logs: Check nginx, apache2, and application log directories. Look for SQL injection attempts, web shells, and unauthorized file uploads. The access log and error log are both important. Check /var/log/nginx/ and /var/log/apache2/.

Crontabs: Persistence mechanism favorites. Check /etc/crontab, /etc/cron.d/, /var/spool/cron/crontabs/, and /etc/cron.daily/. Attackers add reverse shells or download commands to cron. Also check systemd timers with systemctl list-timers.

Rootkit Detection

Check for rootkits with chkrootkit and rkhunter. Verify system binaries have not been replaced by comparing hashes against the package manager expected values. On Debian, use debsums --changed. On RHEL, use rpm -Va to verify all packages.

Compare the output of ps, netstat, and ls against /proc to detect hidden processes or connections. Rootkits that modify these tools will show inconsistencies. Also check /proc/*/exe symlinks for deleted binaries, which indicate process injection or replacement.

Look for hidden kernel modules with lsmod and compare against /proc/modules. Check for modified system calls by examining /proc/kallsyms for unexpected entries. Hidden network connections can be found with ss -tlnp instead of netstat, as some rootkits only hook the netstat binary.

Post-Incident

After investigation, rotate all credentials including passwords, API keys, SSH keys, and database connection strings. The attacker likely exfiltrated whatever they could access. Update and patch the system, implement the security controls that were missing, and document everything for the incident report.

For legal proceedings, maintain a chain of custody document: who collected the evidence, when, how, and where it was stored. Use write-blocking hardware for disk imaging when possible. Hash all evidence files and verify hashes before and after analysis.

Finally, conduct a lessons-learned review. What was the initial attack vector? How long was the attacker present before detection? What controls would have prevented or detected the compromise sooner? Use these findings to improve your monitoring and response procedures for the next incident.
